newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's government set to approve tough budget.
newsitem.headline: Italy's government set to approve tough budget.

text.p: Italy's government was poised to approve a deficit-cutting budget on Friday in a dash to join a European single currency but critics said the middle class was being asked to pay too heavy a burden in new taxes.

A government source said the 1997 budget package would aim to sharply cut a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's public sector deficit, making it one of the most stringent in recent years.
The main portion of the budget would comprise 25 trillion lire in spending cuts and 12.5 trillion lire in fresh revenues.

A further 12.5 trillion lire would be raised from a once-off "Euro-tax" and another 12.5 trillion from unspecified "treasury operations". Full details were expected to be disclosed after a cabinet meeting being chaired by Prime Minister Romano Prodi.

Diego Masi, the parliamentary leader of Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini's centrist Italian Renewal party, resigned in protest on Friday saying the government had caved in to pressure from hard-left leader Fausto Bertinotti.

Prodi has quietly dropped plans to tax pensions and raise charges for hospital treatment after Bertinotti threatened to scupper the budget in parliament. The centre-left government relies on support from Bertinotti's Marxist-inspired Communist Refoundation in the lower house.
"We have given in today to blackmail from Communist Refoundation," Masi said in a resignation letter. He described the budget as "made up entirely of taxes."

The planned budget is far in excess of the 32.4 trillion lire the government originally intended to shave from the public sector deficit and aims to cut Italy's deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio to three percent by the end of next year.
Achievement of the three percent deficit target would put Italy on course to join an advance party of countries establishing a single European currency in 1999.

The government is gambling that an uncompromising budget will give Italy's independent central bank the cue to send interest rates tumbling. That would ease the crushing burden of interest payments on the country's huge national debt.

But critics cautioned that the raft of planned new taxes would hit Italy's salary-earning middle classes hardest, further alienating them from the government, and could also send an already weak economy spinning into recession.
"The compromise over state accounts...will be paid for above all by the middle class," said political analyst Stefano Folli in a commentary in the Milan newspaper Corriere della Sera.

The main champion of budgetary rigour is widely seen to be Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, who is reported to have agreed only reluctantly to drop plans for a "solidarity tax" on pensions and for higher healthcare charges.
Ciampi said in a front-page article in Friday's Corriere that Italy had to deliver a credible budget if it wanted to secure a lasting fall in interest rates.

"We have a duty to generate credibility. It is the path to reduce interest rates and therefore the deficit," Ciampi said, adding that Italy had the most to gain from joining the planned European single currency, the Euro.

"Italy is the country which will receive the biggest dividend from the Euro. If we are in the Euro, the fall in interest rates will free up resources for production, investment and employment," Ciampi added.
